source.title: Scaling Laws For Dense Retrieval
source.authors: Yan Fang; Jingtao Zhan; Qing-Yao Ai; Jia-Xin Mao; Wei-Hang Su; Jia Chen; Yi-Qun Liu

page_placements.theme: Learning curves can exhibit multiple regimes and metric-induced transitions

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to fine-tuned dense retrieval models, measuring contrastive entropy against model size and annotation volume rather than testing language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own dense-retrieval scaling sweeps and resource-allocation predictions. It also discusses scaling laws from prior work, which are not recorded as results. Individual model-point values are mostly shown only in figures; the rows below capture the reported aggregate fits and stated comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of a loss-like metric (test contrastive entropy) for pretrained BERT and ERNIE encoders fine-tuned for dense retrieval. It varies model size (0.5–87M non-embedding parameters) and annotation count. That is a new fine-tuning setting with its own results on whether the power-law form holds (V5), on whether downstream retrieval performance scales predictably with encoder size (V6), and on whether fitted exponents depend on setup (V7). It does not measure language-model pretraining loss, so V1–V4 are not tested directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that contrastive entropy of dense retrievers follows a precise power law in model size and annotation count across datasets and annotation methods, and that a joint N–D law fits and predicts within a certain range. They say the laws can guide budget allocation and the evaluation of annotation methods. They add that human annotations perform best and that LLM-generated annotations leave large room for improvement.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of measuring language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy across parameter, token, and compute scales, the study fine-tunes pretrained encoders for dense retrieval and measures contrastive entropy against model size and annotated-pair count.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted data-size exponent differs between MSMARCO (1.05) and T2Ranking (0.50); annotation methods also differ in slope, with ICT reported as the smallest. The paper notes that results may depend on training techniques and architecture variants not tested.

fits_no_version.finding: The modeled loss-minimising retriever size under a monetary budget moves from about 13B parameters (inference excluded, $20k) to million-scale (inference included). This rests on assumed cost factors and on extrapolating the fit far beyond the 87M maximum tested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For dense retrieval, including corpus-encoding inference cost in the budget shifts the predicted optimal model size from billions to millions of parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard ranking metrics show a sharp improvement around a contrastive-entropy threshold of about 0.25, which the authors call emergent ranking ability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Discrete retrieval metrics change abruptly at a threshold of a continuous retrieval loss, even when the loss scales smoothly.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR ’24)
record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty intervals for the scaling fits. Its experiments cover two in-domain datasets and model sizes up to 87 million parameters; the authors say larger scales and out-of-domain evaluation remain unresolved. Contrastive entropy is not equivalent to ranking metrics, and Section 4.3 contains conflicting statements about whether ChatGLM3-generated annotations surpass human annotations at 500k.

untested.parts: All of it. The study measures held-out contrastive entropy after retrieval fine-tuning, not language-model pretraining loss.

All of it. Held-out joint-fit points are only described as 'relatively close' within the tested range. There is no extrapolation across orders of magnitude, and the 13B budget optimum is never trained.
All of it. Only a monetary budget model for retrieval is given, with no compute-optimal parameter/token analysis.
There is no controlled fixed-N shape comparison of pretraining loss. BERT shape variants are only plotted on the fine-tuned model-size curve.

Untested: other modalities, repeated data, and transfer. Also untested: out-of-domain retrieval (the authors attempted it but did not report it as unstable), sophisticated training techniques (hard negatives, distillation), and model sizes above 87M.
Downstream performance against pretraining loss, other downstream tasks, and out-of-domain retrieval.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedules (fixed at 10,000 steps), curvature away from a power law, and disagreement between the published LM laws.

missing.what: BERT shape variants (different attention heads and feed-forward dimensions) are plotted on the model-size curve and described as lying along it. This bears on the shape-insensitivity idea in a fine-tuned setting, but no row records it.
missing.versions: V5 (and V4-like, though V4 strictly concerns pretraining loss)

missing.what: The ranges actually spanned: annotation counts of about 100K–500K (MSMARCO) and 100K–700K (T2Ranking), and model size of 0.5–82/87M. Researchers need these to judge how strongly a power law is established.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. Evidence is limited: the only measure is a contrastive loss after fine-tuning, model sizes reach at most 87M, data ranges are narrow, and no uncertainty is reported. The best test-set loss across training is reported, which selects on the test set. The Figure 5 caption contradicts the Section 4.3 prose on ChatGLM3 versus human annotations. The study is peer reviewed (SIGIR '24) and its code is released.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures contrastive entropy after dense-retrieval fine-tuning, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
The paper makes some predictions for dense-retrieval performance, but does not test whether language-model loss predictions from small runs extrapolate to runs orders of magnitude larger.

Its budget analysis allocates money among retrieval-model size, annotations, training, and inference; it does not test parameter and token scaling under a fixed compute budget or compare their growth powers.
It notes BERT variants differ in architecture, but does not report a controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests dense-retrieval fine-tuning on English and Chinese datasets and several annotation types; does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, or fine-tuning/transfer regimes beyond this dense-retrieval setting.

Tests dense-retrieval task performance using contrastive entropy and its association with ranking metrics; does not test downstream task performance across language-model pretraining scales or against pretraining loss.

Reports different data-size exponents across datasets and annotation methods, but does not vary fitting methods or parameter-count conventions, assess disagreement among the cited language-model laws, or test curves bending away from power laws.

rows.subject: Dense retrieval models trained with ICT-generated annotations (aggregate curve)
rows.operation_detail: Varied annotation count and fitted contrastive entropy for the ICT-generated annotation condition.
rows.value: figure only; text says ICT has the smallest slope among the three query-generation methods
rows.note: The paper says ICT is low-quality weak supervision and limits the improvement from increasing data.
rows.check: The state should be observed, not partial. ICT is still fitted by a power law (Eq. 7); only its slope is smallest. A smaller exponent is evidence for V7's setup-dependence, not a weaker V5 effect. Drop V6.

rows.subject: ChatGLM3-annotation condition compared with human annotations
rows.operation_detail: Compared annotation-condition performance at the largest reported annotation count.
rows.value: Figure 5 caption says ChatGLM3 annotations surpass human annotations at 500k
rows.note: This caption conflicts with the prose in Section 4.3, which says human annotations lead to the best-performing models.
rows.check: This row compares annotation sources at a single data size; it does not bear on the power-law form. The Figure 5 caption says ChatGLM3 surpasses human annotations at 500k. The prose says human annotations are best and docT5query beats ChatGLM3. The value cannot be read reliably.

rows.subject: BERT model-size and annotation-count combinations (aggregate joint fit)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained checkpoints fine-tuned on retrieval annotations
rows.operation_detail: Fitted a joint model-size and data-size function and compared its predictions with held-out combinations.
rows.measure: Joint fit and prediction of contrastive entropy from model size and annotation count
rows.value: A ≈ 3.6 × 10^4, B ≈ 7.1 × 10^3, α ≈ 0.56, β ≈ 1.31, δ ≈ 0.03; authors say predictions are relatively close to observed values
rows.note: The paper does not state that these predictions cover runs orders of magnitude larger.
rows.check: Add V7. The joint fit on the same MSMARCO data gives β≈1.31 and α≈0.56, against 1.05 and 0.53 from the single-factor fits. This shows exponent dependence on the fitting form. The held-out prediction points are not shown to be orders of magnitude larger, so V2 is not tested.

rows.check: The link and state are fine. The correlation is strong and near linear, but ranking metrics jump near 0.25 contrastive entropy. The authors say similar entropy does not guarantee similar ranking. Values are figure only.
